title: There was SO much I didn’t get to talk about in the video because La ...
transcript: theater kids lock in we're going to the movies this one you could watch from home but I'd recommend if you can to go see it in a theater LA Negra is one of the most visually stunning and ambitious films I saw at TIFF just inspired by theater but is literally built around it based on two plays but then also Rodrigo Garcia Lorca Lorca is one of Spain's most celebrated poets and playwrights he was also a gay man who was assassinated just at the beginning of the Spanish Civil War and when he died he left behind an unfinished play called LA Bola Negra and only four pages have survived rather than simply trying to imagine how that play would finish directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrosi use those four pages alongside other of Lorca's works and his legacy more broadly as the foundation to this huge historical queer epic that spans across three different timelines some of it is true and some of it is fictional this movie is so patient it lets each story breathe on its own it gives you these characters and their desires and their fears and these three different worlds that they are trying to navigate and by the time you see the larger picture everything the movie has been building towards becomes more powerful what does it cost to hide who you are and what are people willing to do to simply survive this is a story that is about queerness and identity and how while the world may change and evolve these desires that we have for love for acceptance for authenticity and freedom and safety they don't change Javier Aires directed the hell out of this film it's incredibly theatrical the performances are absolutely phenomenal so sorry about your name one of the most nuanced beautiful performances I've ever seen this was his very first acting role so many moments of quiet where he's unable to say what he wants to say where he's not allowed to say what he wants to say and yet you know exactly what he's feeling because you see it in his eyes he plays opposite Miguel Binardo again sorry their relationship is so complex and intimate I love them I love them and then anchoring the other two timelines you have Milo Kyles and Carlo Gonzalez just so wonderful and like this entire ensemble you don't see them together on screen they feel so connected and unsurprisingly Penelope Cruz who is in a handful of scenes she is one of the most compelling actresses to watch she sings she dances I didn't know she could do everything there is a lot happening in LA Bola Negra and what I keep thinking about is that Lorca was murdered his work remained unfinished one of the countless queer people throughout history whose stories were hidden suppressed or erased entirely what LA Bola Negra does is remind us that art can give them the space to exist again I walked out of TIFF feeling like I'd only started to process this film I really want to see it again there is going to be a limited theatrical run and then it'll be on Netflix starting December 2nd I'm so so glad I got to see this movie
